gloss_terse: Rumah — a place name appearing in the account of King Jehoiakim's lineage
gloss_readable: Rumah is a place name mentioned only in connection with Zebudah, the mother of King Jehoiakim. The location is identified as the hometown of Jehoiakim's mother. The Septuagint offers varied transliterations (Krouma, Ryma, Lobenna), suggesting uncertainty about the precise location even in antiquity. Some scholars have connected it with Arumah in Judges 9:41, though this remains speculative.

senses.1: A town in Israel, mentioned as the birthplace or residence of Zebudah (2 Kings 23:36). The exact location remains uncertain, though possible connections with Arumah have been suggested. The varied ancient translations reflect geographical ambiguity that persisted into the Hellenistic period.

gloss_terse: haughtily — with arrogant bearing, in an elevated or prideful manner
gloss_readable: This rare adverb describes a manner of walking characterized by pride and arrogance. In Micah 2:3, it appears in God's warning that the people will no longer walk haughtily because judgment is coming. The word connects to the root meaning of 'height' or 'elevation,' suggesting a lifted posture or attitude. The Spanish and English renderings ('erguidos,' 'haughtily') both capture this sense of arrogant bearing that will be brought low.

senses.1: Describes walking or moving with pride and arrogance, literally 'with lifted head' or elevated posture (Micah 2:3). The adverb characterizes an attitude of haughtiness that God promises to humble. This single biblical occurrence forms part of a prophetic oracle about coming judgment that will prevent such prideful behavior.

gloss_terse: exaltation — praise, extolling, or song of praise directed to God
gloss_readable: This term denotes praise or exaltation, particularly in the context of worship directed to Yahweh. In Psalm 66:17, it appears as 'exaltation was under my tongue,' describing the psalmist's readiness to praise. Some manuscripts read this as a verb form rather than a noun, but most lexicographers favor understanding it as referring to a song of praise. The root connects to the concept of lifting up or elevating, here applied to vocal worship that elevates God's name.

senses.1: A song of praise or act of exaltation directed toward Yahweh (Psalm 66:17). The term captures the worshiper's readiness to vocally lift up God's name. Cross-linguistically rendered as 'exaltation' in Spanish, French, and German, this word emphasizes the lifting nature of praise that honors the divine.

gloss_terse: exaltations — praises, songs of exaltation (plural construct form)
gloss_readable: This plural construct form refers to multiple acts or expressions of exaltation and praise. In Psalm 149:6, it appears as 'the exaltations of God in their throat,' describing how the faithful carry songs of praise ready on their lips. The plural form suggests abundant, repeated, or varied expressions of worship. Like its singular counterpart, this term connects praise to the imagery of elevation and lifting up.

senses.1: Multiple songs of praise or exaltations of God (Psalm 149:6). The phrase 'exaltations of God' suggests praise ready to be voiced, carried in the throat of the worshipers. This construct plural emphasizes the abundance and readiness of praise among the faithful community.

gloss_terse: tremble — to shake, quiver, or rock back and forth
gloss_readable: This verb describes a shaking or trembling motion, used metaphorically in Job 26:11 where 'the pillars of heaven tremble' at God's rebuke. The root appears in Aramaic and Arabic with similar meanings of gentle movement, quivering, or fluttering. The image is one of cosmic structures shaking before divine power. The translation consensus across languages ('tremble,' 'tiemblan') reflects this sense of involuntary shaking in response to overwhelming force.

senses.1: To shake, tremble, or rock, particularly describing the cosmic pillars of heaven that quiver at God's rebuke (Job 26:11). The verb conveys involuntary trembling before divine power, with cognates in Aramaic and Arabic suggesting gentle rocking or quivering motion. The poetic image emphasizes the foundational structures of creation shaking before God.

gloss_terse: flowing — to flow or run, especially of bodily discharges
gloss_readable: This verb describes the flowing or running of liquids, used specifically in Leviticus 15:3 for a bodily discharge. The root appears in Aramaic for saliva or spittle, and in Arabic for slobbering or slavering. The Hebrew usage focuses on the continuous flow of a discharge from the body, with medical or ritual purity implications. The verb captures the ongoing nature of the flow rather than a single emission.

senses.1: To flow or run continuously, used of bodily discharge in ritual purity contexts (Leviticus 15:3). The phrase 'his flesh flows with his discharge' describes an ongoing condition rather than a single event. Aramaic and Arabic cognates referring to saliva and slobbering support the sense of liquid flowing from the body.

gloss_terse: Rezon — the founder of an Aramean kingdom in Damascus during Solomon's reign
gloss_readable: Rezon was an adversary of Solomon who established himself as king in Damascus. First Kings 11:23 identifies him as a military leader who broke away and founded an independent kingdom. Some scholars have attempted to identify him with Hezion mentioned in 1 Kings 15:18, though this remains uncertain. The Septuagint's varied renderings (Esrom, Razon) reflect the challenge of transliterating Semitic names into Greek.

senses.1: A personal name: the founder of an Aramean kingdom centered in Damascus who opposed Solomon's rule (1 Kings 11:23). Rezon represents one of several adversaries who arose during Solomon's later years, challenging Israelite regional dominance. Proposed identifications with Hezion remain speculative.

gloss_terse: prince, potentate — a ruler or person of high rank and authority
gloss_readable: This term denotes a ruler or potentate, appearing in parallel with 'king' in Proverbs 14:28. The verse states that 'in a multitude of people is a king's glory, but in the lack of people is a prince's ruin.' The parallelism suggests someone of royal or high political rank. The root may connect to concepts of wealth or abundance, fitting the context of population size as a measure of a ruler's strength.

senses.1: A prince, potentate, or ruler of high rank (Proverbs 14:28). The term appears in parallel with 'king,' suggesting comparable authority. The context emphasizes that a ruler's power depends on having many subjects—without people, even a prince faces ruin. Spanish and English translations converge on 'prince' or 'príncipe.'

gloss_terse: flash, wink — to flash or blink the eyes, possibly in anger
gloss_readable: This verb describes a flashing or winking motion of the eyes, used in Job 15:12 where Eliphaz asks Job, 'Why do your eyes flash?' The context suggests anger or agitation. The root appears as a transposition of an Arabic and Aramaic root meaning to signal or make signs. Some manuscripts have variant readings, and some scholars suggest emending to a more common verb for 'lifted eyes,' but the sense of eye movement expressing emotion remains central.

senses.1: To flash or wink with the eyes, expressing anger or agitation (Job 15:12). Eliphaz's rhetorical question 'Why do your eyes flash?' challenges Job's emotional display during their debate. The verb captures involuntary eye movement that betrays inner turmoil, with cognates in Aramaic and Arabic related to signaling or gesturing.

gloss_terse: far — distant, remote, at a distance (Aramaic)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic adjective means 'far' or 'distant,' appearing in Ezra 6:6 in the command to 'keep far from there.' The Persian decree orders Tattenai and his associates to stay away from the temple construction in Jerusalem. The Aramaic form reflects the administrative language of the Persian Empire used in official correspondence. The command emphasizes complete separation and non-interference.

senses.1: Far, distant, or remote (Ezra 6:6). Used in the imperial command to Persian officials to 'keep far from' the Jerusalem temple site, emphasizing non-interference with the Jewish rebuilding project. This Aramaic administrative term reflects the multilingual nature of Persian-era governance documents.

gloss_terse: Raham — a personal name in the genealogy of Judah
gloss_readable: Raham is listed in the genealogical records of Judah in 1 Chronicles 2:44. The name may derive from a root related to 'compassion' or possibly 'girl' or 'maiden,' though its exact etymology is uncertain. The Septuagint provides varied Greek transliterations (Ramee, Raem, Raam), typical of personal names. The individual's role beyond this genealogical mention is unknown.

senses.1: A personal name appearing in Judah's genealogy (1 Chronicles 2:44). The name's etymology may connect to roots meaning 'compassion' or 'maiden,' though this remains uncertain. The varied Septuagint renderings reflect the challenge of transliterating Hebrew personal names into Greek. No narrative details about this individual survive.

gloss_terse: compassion — mercy, tender feelings, pity (Aramaic plural intensive)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic plural intensive noun means 'compassion' or 'mercy,' appearing in Daniel 2:18 where Daniel and his companions seek compassion from the God of heaven regarding Nebuchadnezzar's dream. The plural intensive form (like Hebrew rahamim) emphasizes the depth and abundance of divine mercy. The term connects to the same root as 'womb,' suggesting tender, maternal care. This is the language of urgent prayer for divine intervention.

senses.1: Compassion, mercy, or tender feelings in intensive plural form (Daniel 2:18). Daniel and his friends seek 'compassion from the God of heaven' facing a death sentence. The Aramaic plural intensive (like Hebrew rahamim) suggests abundant, deep mercy. The root connection to 'womb' evokes maternal tenderness applied to God's character.

gloss_terse: womb — the female reproductive organ; metaphorically, the place of origin or birth
gloss_readable: This common term for the womb appears throughout Scripture in both literal and metaphorical contexts. It can refer to the physical organ of childbirth, to birth itself ('from the womb'), or figuratively to origins and beginnings. The dual form in Judges 5:30 ('a womb, two wombs for each man') uses crude language for captured women, reflecting the brutal reality of ancient warfare. The word frequently appears in expressions about God's sovereignty over conception and birth.

senses.1: The dual form 'two wombs' appears in Judges 5:30 in the anticipated victory song of Sisera's mother, crudely referring to captured women as spoils of war. This rare dual construction emphasizes the dehumanizing language of military conquest. The term reflects the harsh reality that women were considered plunder in ancient Near Eastern warfare.

gloss_terse: compassionate — showing mercy, tender-hearted, merciful (feminine plural adjective)
gloss_readable: This adjective describes people characterized by compassion or mercy. In Lamentations 4:10, it appears in the shocking phrase 'compassionate women' who cooked their own children during the siege of Jerusalem. The irony is devastating—women whose nature should be tender and merciful were driven by extreme famine to unthinkable acts. The adjective derives from the same root as 'womb,' suggesting natural maternal tenderness that the siege conditions perverted.

senses.1: Compassionate or tender-hearted, describing women (Lamentations 4:10). The phrase 'compassionate women' appears in one of Scripture's most horrifying images: mothers cooking their own children during Jerusalem's siege. The tragic irony intensifies the horror—those naturally most tender-hearted were driven to the most unnatural acts by extreme famine.

gloss_terse: tremble — to grow soft, relax, or shake (of bones in fear)
gloss_readable: This verb means to grow soft, relax, or tremble, used in Jeremiah 23:9 where the prophet describes his physical response to God's words: 'all my bones trembled.' The context is Jeremiah's overwhelming reaction to prophetic revelation about judgment on false prophets. The Arabic cognate suggests softness or limpness, fitting the image of bones that have lost their strength. The verb captures the physical manifestation of being appalled or terrified.

senses.1: To grow soft, relax, or tremble, describing bones that shake in fear or shock (Jeremiah 23:9). Jeremiah's declaration 'all my bones trembled' expresses his physical response to God's words of judgment. The verb suggests a loss of rigidity or strength, as if the skeletal structure itself becomes weak before divine revelation. Arabic cognates meaning 'soft' support this sense of structural weakening.

gloss_terse: trust — to rely on, have confidence in, set one's trust upon (Aramaic)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic verb means to trust or have confidence in someone or something. In Daniel 3:28, Nebuchadnezzar blesses the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego because they 'trusted in Him' and defied the king's command rather than worship other gods. The Hithpael form suggests reflexive action—they set their own trust upon God. This is the language of radical reliance that accepts even death rather than compromise. Cognates appear in Syriac and Assyrian with similar meanings of trust and reliance.

senses.1: To trust, rely on, or set one's confidence in God (Daniel 3:28). The three young men 'trusted' in God and refused to worship the golden image, even facing death in the furnace. This Aramaic Hithpael form emphasizes their deliberate, reflexive act of placing trust in God over royal commands. The verb captures absolute reliance that risks everything.

gloss_terse: those departing — those who are far from, those who remove themselves (participle as substantive)
gloss_readable: This verbal adjective functions as a noun meaning 'those who depart' or 'those who are far from.' In Psalm 73:27, it describes 'those who are far from You' (God)—people who remove themselves from divine presence and relationship. The form captures ongoing action: not just distant, but actively departing or removing oneself. The context contrasts those who abandon God with the psalmist who draws near. This is spiritual geography—relational distance from God.

senses.1: Those who depart from or are far from God, used as a substantive participle (Psalm 73:27). The phrase 'those far from You' describes people who actively remove themselves from God's presence. The participial form suggests ongoing action rather than static distance—continuous departure rather than mere remoteness. The psalmist declares that such people perish while he draws near.

gloss_terse: overflow, be astir — to bubble up, boil over, stir with words or emotion
gloss_readable: This verb means to stir, move, or overflow, used in Psalm 45:1 where the psalmist says 'my heart overflows with a good word.' The image is of something bubbling up from within, like boiling liquid. Aramaic and Syriac cognates suggest creeping, moving, or fluttering, while the Talmudic usage connects to the movement of lips in speech. The French translation 'bouillir' (to boil) captures the sense of something bubbling forth, here applied to inspired speech that wells up from the heart.

senses.1: To overflow, bubble up, or be astir with words or emotion (Psalm 45:1). The psalmist's heart 'overflows with a good word' like liquid boiling over, unable to be contained. This is inspired speech that wells up from within, described with imagery of movement and stirring. The verb captures the irrepressible nature of the poet's composition for the king.

gloss_terse: winnowing shovel — an agricultural tool for separating grain from chaff
gloss_readable: This term refers to a winnowing shovel or similar agricultural implement used to separate grain from chaff. In Isaiah 30:24, it appears alongside a fork in the description of how animals will eat grain 'winnowed with shovel and fork.' The exact nature of the tool is uncertain—proposals include ventilating fan (from the root for 'wind'), something soft or friable, or simply a broad shovel. The context clearly indicates agricultural processing of grain for animal feed.

senses.1: A winnowing shovel or agricultural tool for separating grain (Isaiah 30:24). Paired with 'fork,' this implement processes grain that will feed working animals. The root etymology is uncertain—possibly from 'wind' (suggesting a fanning tool) or from 'soft/friable' (suggesting its function). Cross-linguistic evidence shows this as a borrowed term in Arabic, indicating cultural exchange of agricultural technology.

gloss_terse: be wet, be moist — to be drenched or moistened
gloss_readable: This verb means to be moist or wet, used in Job 24:8 to describe the poor who 'are wet with mountain rain' and have no shelter. The root appears broadly in Semitic languages (Assyrian, Arabic, Ethiopic, Aramaic, Syriac) with the consistent meaning of moisture. The image is of people exposed to the elements, drenched by rain because they lack housing. Job's complaint emphasizes the vulnerability of the destitute who cannot escape the weather.

senses.1: To be wet, moist, or drenched by water (Job 24:8). The verse describes the poor 'wet with mountain rain,' lacking shelter from the elements. This verb captures the physical condition of exposure—bodies soaked by rain because there is no refuge. The widespread Semitic cognates confirm this as a basic term for moisture or wetness.

gloss_terse: moist, juicy, fresh — full of sap, green, thriving
gloss_readable: This adjective means moist, juicy, or fresh, describing something full of vitality and sap. In Job 8:16, it characterizes a plant that 'is moist before the sun'—green, thriving, and full of life. The word emphasizes the fresh, sap-filled condition of a healthy plant in contrast to withered vegetation. The imagery serves Bildad's argument about the fate of those who forget God—like plants, they may seem fresh temporarily but will dry up without proper foundation.

senses.1: Moist, juicy, fresh, or full of sap, describing a thriving plant (Job 8:16). The phrase 'he is moist before the sun' depicts a plant in its prime—green, sap-filled, and vigorous. This condition of vitality serves as a metaphor in Bildad's speech, contrasting temporary appearance of health with ultimate withering for those without God. Spanish 'jugoso' (juicy) captures the sense of sap-filled freshness.

gloss_terse: trembling, panic — sudden fear, shaking terror
gloss_readable: This noun means trembling or panic, appearing in Jeremiah 49:24 in the oracle against Damascus: 'panic has seized her.' The term describes sudden, overwhelming fear that takes hold of a person or city facing judgment. The verb form suggests that panic grips or seizes—an active force that overcomes resistance. This is not gradual anxiety but sudden terror in the face of imminent disaster.

senses.1: Trembling or panic, sudden overwhelming fear (Jeremiah 49:24). The phrase describes Damascus gripped by terror as judgment approaches: 'panic has seized her.' This is fear that overcomes and paralyzes, an involuntary physical and emotional response to impending disaster. The verb 'seize' emphasizes panic as an external force that takes hold.

gloss_terse: grow fresh — to become fresh, rejuvenated, or restored (of flesh)
gloss_readable: This rare quadriliteral verb means to grow fresh or rejuvenated. In Job 33:25, it describes restored health: 'his flesh grows fresher than in youth.' Elihu speaks of divine restoration where diseased or aged flesh becomes young again. The verb's exact etymology is uncertain—possibly a transposition of a root meaning 'wide, loose, delicate' or 'fat.' The Talmud uses related forms for fatty tissue, while Arabic suggests convalescence. The image is of reversal: aged or sick flesh restored to youthful vitality.

senses.1: To grow fresh, be rejuvenated, or become renewed, specifically of flesh or bodily health (Job 33:25). Elihu describes divine healing where 'his flesh grows fresher than in youth'—complete restoration to youthful vigor. The passive form suggests transformation that happens to someone rather than something they do. This rare verb may be a transposition from roots meaning 'fat' or 'delicate,' emphasizing healthy tissue.

gloss_terse: moisture — wetness, water content
gloss_readable: This noun means moisture or wetness, appearing in Job 37:11 in Elihu's speech about weather: 'He burdens the cloud with moisture.' The term refers to the water content that clouds carry, making them heavy before releasing rain. The root connects to the verb for 'being wet' or 'saturated.' The image is of God loading clouds with water, controlling the precipitation cycle. This fits the broader passage about divine governance of natural phenomena.

senses.1: Moisture or water content, particularly in clouds (Job 37:11). The phrase 'He burdens the cloud with moisture' describes God loading clouds with water before rain. This meteorological term emphasizes the weight of water vapor that clouds carry. The context celebrates divine control over weather patterns and the water cycle.

gloss_terse: smell, odor — scent, particularly absence of smell (Aramaic)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic noun means smell or odor, appearing in Daniel 3:27 in the phrase 'the smell of fire had not come upon them.' After Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego emerge from the furnace, observers note that not even the scent of fire clings to them—their clothes, hair, and bodies show no trace of smoke or burning. The term emphasizes the completeness of their miraculous preservation: not just survival, but total absence of any effect from the fire.

senses.1: Smell or odor, specifically scent of fire (Daniel 3:27). The phrase 'the smell of fire had not come upon them' emphasizes the miraculous nature of the three men's deliverance—no trace of smoke or burning remained on their bodies or clothes. This Aramaic term highlights complete preservation: even the odor of their ordeal was absent. The detail intensifies the wonder of divine protection.

gloss_terse: Diphath — a descendant of Japheth, son of Gomer (variant spelling)
gloss_readable: Diphath appears in 1 Chronicles 1:6 as a son of Gomer and descendant of Japheth in the Table of Nations. This is a variant spelling of Riphath, which appears in the parallel passage in Genesis 10:3. The variation between 'D' and 'R' in Hebrew script is minimal and easily confused, explaining the textual variant. The Septuagint transliterations (Eriphath, Riphae, Riphath) show the same person referenced across manuscripts with slight spelling differences.

senses.1: A personal name: son of Gomer and grandson of Japheth in the Table of Nations (1 Chronicles 1:6). This represents a variant spelling of Riphath (Genesis 10:3), with the initial consonant difference reflecting scribal variation. The Septuagint's varied transliterations confirm these refer to the same individual. No additional information about this descendant of Japheth survives beyond genealogical mention.

gloss_terse: Riphath — a descendant of Japheth, son of Gomer
gloss_readable: Riphath appears in Genesis 10:3 as a son of Gomer and grandson of Japheth in the Table of Nations. The parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 1:6 has the variant Diphath. Josephus identified this lineage with the Paphlagonians of Asia Minor. Some scholars connect the name to the Rhebas River (modern Riva) on the Thracian Bosphorus, suggesting a geographic connection. The exact ethnic or geographic referent remains uncertain, though a northern or northwestern Asia Minor location seems likely.

senses.1: A personal name: son of Gomer and grandson of Japheth (Genesis 10:3). Ancient interpreters like Josephus associated this lineage with Paphlagonia in northern Asia Minor. Some scholars connect the name to the Rhebas River on the Thracian Bosphorus. The Table of Nations uses personal names to represent ethnic groups or geographic regions, so Riphath likely designates a people or territory in northwestern Anatolia.

gloss_terse: tenderness, delicacy — softness, refinement, gentle upbringing
gloss_readable: This noun means tenderness or delicacy, describing the refined, soft condition of someone raised in comfort. In Deuteronomy 28:56, it characterizes 'the most tender and delicate woman among you'—someone so pampered and refined that she has never set foot on the ground. The term appears in the curses of the covenant, describing how even such refined people will be reduced to cannibalism during siege. The word emphasizes gentle upbringing and physical softness from a life of luxury.

senses.1: Tenderness, delicacy, or softness from refined upbringing (Deuteronomy 28:56). The phrase 'from tenderness and delicacy' describes a woman so pampered she has never touched her foot to the ground. This physical softness from luxurious living serves to intensify the horror of the siege curses—even the most delicate will commit atrocities. The term captures refinement that prosperity produces but adversity destroys.

gloss_terse: riding — the act of riding, riding equipment or saddle cloths
gloss_readable: This noun refers to the act of riding or possibly riding equipment such as saddle cloths. In Ezekiel 27:20, Dedan trades with Tyre 'in saddle cloths for riding.' The exact reference is uncertain—either the activity of riding (abstract noun) or the equipment used for riding (concrete). The context of international trade suggests luxury riding equipment, which would be valuable trade goods. The term connects to the common verb for riding on animals.

senses.1: The act of riding or saddle cloths/riding equipment (Ezekiel 27:20). Dedan supplies Tyre with items 'for riding,' either referring to the activity itself or to valuable saddle blankets and riding gear. The commercial context favors understanding this as trade goods—luxury riding equipment rather than the abstract concept. This reflects the importance of mounted travel and quality riding apparatus in ancient trade networks.

gloss_terse: Recah — a place name in the territory of Judah
gloss_readable: Recah is a place name mentioned in 1 Chronicles 4:12 within the genealogical records of Judah. The exact location is unknown, and the site has not been identified with any confidence. The Septuagint transliterates it as Rechab, which has led to some textual confusion with the personal name Rechab. The name appears in a list of settlements or descendants associated with Judah's territory, but no narrative details about the place survive.

senses.1: A place name in Judah's genealogical records (1 Chronicles 4:12). The location has not been identified, and no details about the settlement survive beyond this genealogical mention. The Septuagint's rendering as 'Rechab' shows the overlap between personal and place names in Hebrew genealogies. This may represent a town, clan, or family settlement within Judah's territory.

gloss_terse: chariot — a riding vehicle, divine chariot (poetic)
gloss_readable: This poetic term for chariot appears in Psalm 104:3, describing God 'who makes the clouds His chariot.' The Aramaic-influenced form suggests a vehicle for riding, here used metaphorically for God's transportation through the heavens. The image of divine cloud-riding appears elsewhere in ancient Near Eastern literature, particularly Canaanite texts about Baal. The psalmist appropriates this imagery for Yahweh, emphasizing His mastery over creation and His mobility through the sky on storm clouds.

senses.1: A chariot or riding vehicle, used poetically of God's cloud-chariot (Psalm 104:3). The phrase 'who makes the clouds His chariot' depicts God riding through the heavens on storm clouds. This royal imagery of cloud-riding draws on ancient Near Eastern motifs while applying them to Yahweh. The Aramaic-influenced term emphasizes the vehicle aspect, picturing clouds as God's mobile throne-chariot.

gloss_terse: Racal — a place in southern Judah (possibly textual error for Carmel)
gloss_readable: Racal appears in 1 Samuel 30:29 as a town in southern Judah where David sent spoils after defeating the Amalekites. However, most scholars believe this is a textual error for Carmel, since the Septuagint reads 'Carmel' and Carmel is well-known as a town in this region. The similarity in Hebrew script between Racal and Carmel makes scribal confusion plausible. If Racal is original, no other references to this town exist. The context involves David distributing plunder to allies in southern Judah.

senses.1: A place name in southern Judah mentioned in David's distribution of spoils (1 Samuel 30:29). Most scholars consider this a scribal error for Carmel, supported by the Septuagint reading 'Carmel' and the well-attested presence of Carmel in this region. If original, Racal would be an otherwise unknown town in Judah's southern territory. The name appears only in this context of David rewarding his allies.

gloss_terse: rough places — rugged terrain, mountain ridges, or uneven ground
gloss_readable: This term refers to rough, uneven, or rugged terrain, appearing in Isaiah 40:4 in the promise that 'the rough places shall become level ground.' The exact nuance is debated—proposals include rough ground, mountain ridges, or bound-up/impassable terrain. The context contrasts rough places with valleys, suggesting elevated, broken terrain. The image is of road preparation where obstacles are removed and uneven ground is smoothed. This serves as a metaphor for removing obstacles to God's coming.

senses.1: Rough places, rugged terrain, or mountain ridges that impede travel (Isaiah 40:4). Paired with 'the crooked' and contrasted with 'valley,' this term describes uneven, broken ground. The prophetic promise envisions smoothing rough terrain to prepare a highway—literally for returning exiles, metaphorically for God's coming. Proposed etymologies include 'binding/knots' (suggesting impassable areas) or 'mountain chains' (suggesting ridges).

gloss_terse: conspiracies — plots, schemes, or bands of conspirators
gloss_readable: This noun refers to conspiracies, plots, or possibly bands of conspirators, though its exact meaning remains uncertain. In Psalm 31:20, God hides the faithful 'from the conspiracies of men' in parallel with 'the strife of tongues.' Proposed meanings include snares, leagues, conspiracies, or plotting bands. The context suggests organized opposition or scheming against the righteous. The parallel with 'strife of tongues' points toward verbal plotting or slander. This is human scheming from which God provides refuge.

senses.1: Conspiracies, plots, or schemes of hostile men (Psalm 31:20). God hides the faithful 'from the conspiracies of men' in parallel with verbal attacks ('strife of tongues'). The term suggests organized opposition—either plots, alliances, or bands of conspirators. The exact nuance is debated, but the context clearly indicates hostile human schemes from which God provides shelter. This is social opposition rather than physical attack.

gloss_terse: Ramoth-negev — a place name meaning 'heights of the Negev' in southern Judah
gloss_readable: Ramoth-negev, literally 'heights of the Negev,' appears in 1 Samuel 30:27 as one of the towns in southern Judah where David sent spoils after defeating the Amalekites. The name indicates elevated terrain in the Negev region. This may be the same location as Ramah of the South or Baalath-beer mentioned elsewhere. The site has not been definitively identified. David's distribution of plunder to this and other southern towns helped build political alliances before he became king.

senses.1: A place name meaning 'heights of the Negev,' located in southern Judah (1 Samuel 30:27). David sent spoils from his Amalekite victory to this town, building alliances in the Negev region. The name indicates elevated terrain in the southern wilderness. Possible identification with Ramah of the South or Baalath-beer remains speculative. This was part of David's support network before assuming kingship.

gloss_terse: height, stature — elevated position, loftiness, or physical corpse (uncertain)
gloss_reading: This noun refers to height, loftiness, or stature, though its exact meaning in Ezekiel 32:5 is debated. The verse speaks of scattering Pharaoh's 'height' or possibly 'corpse' on the mountains. If 'height' is meant, it refers to lofty status or pride being brought low. Some translations favor 'carrion' or 'carcass,' understanding the term as referring to Pharaoh's dead body. The Spanish rendering 'carroña' (carrion) reflects this interpretation. The context of judgment and corpses scattered on mountains favors the concrete meaning.

senses.1: Height, lofty stature, or possibly carrion/corpse (Ezekiel 32:5). In the oracle against Pharaoh, God promises to scatter his 'height' or 'carcass' on the mountains. If abstract, this refers to his lofty pride brought low; if concrete, to his corpse defiling the terrain. Spanish 'carroña' and the context of judgment favor understanding this as Pharaoh's dead body scattered in defeat.

gloss_terse: the archers, the Arameans — Syrian forces or possibly bowmen (textual uncertainty)
gloss_readable: This term in 2 Chronicles 22:5 is textually problematic. It could mean 'the Arameans' (Syrians) or possibly 'the archers.' The parallel passage in 2 Kings 8:28-29 and 9:15 clearly has 'Arameans,' supporting the ethnic interpretation. The Hebrew spelling in Chronicles may reflect a scribal variant or confusion with a word for archers. The context involves battle against Aramean forces at Ramoth-gilead. Most modern translations follow the reading 'Arameans' based on the parallel texts.

senses.1: The Arameans or possibly archers (2 Chronicles 22:5). In the battle at Ramoth-gilead, this term refers to enemy forces who wounded Joram. Parallel passages in Kings clearly read 'Arameans,' suggesting this Chronicles spelling is a variant or error. The Syrian forces under Hazael are the historical opponent. Some have proposed 'archers' based on the Hebrew letters, but the ethnic meaning fits the broader narrative.

gloss_terse: Ramiah — a personal name meaning possibly 'Yahweh has loosened or deceived'
gloss_readable: Ramiah is a personal name appearing in Ezra 10:25 in the list of those who had married foreign wives during the exile. The name's etymology is uncertain but possibly means 'Yahweh has loosened' or 'Yahweh has thrown (deceived?).' The individual is listed among those who put away foreign wives in response to Ezra's reform. The Septuagint transliterates the name as Ramias. No other information about this person survives beyond this mention in the post-exilic reform context.

senses.1: A personal name of a man who married a foreign wife (Ezra 10:25). The name possibly means 'Yahweh has loosened' or 'Yahweh has thrown,' though the etymology is uncertain. This individual appears only in the list of those who divorced foreign wives during Ezra's reforms. The name's theological component (incorporating Yahweh) contrasts ironically with the violation of covenant marriage laws.

gloss_terse: royal mares, steeds — swift horses bred for royalty (exact meaning uncertain)
gloss_readable: This term appears in Esther 8:10 describing the horses used for the king's urgent dispatches. The exact meaning is debated—proposed interpretations include 'sons of mares' (suggesting swift horses bred from royal mares), herds of horses, or mules. The word appears to be a foreign loanword, possibly from Persian or Pahlavi, related to herds or flocks. The Syriac cognate means 'herd,' while Persian ramak means a herd of horses or sheep. The context emphasizes speed and royal quality of these animals used for imperial communication.

senses.1: Royal horses, swift steeds, or possibly mules used for urgent royal dispatches (Esther 8:10). The phrase 'sons of the royal mares' likely indicates horses bred for speed and quality. This is a foreign loanword, probably Persian, related to herds or flocks of animals. The context emphasizes rapid communication throughout the Persian Empire using the finest available horses. The exact species (horses vs. mules) remains debated.

gloss_terse: uplifting, arising — the act of rising up or being exalted
gloss_readable: This noun refers to uplifting, arising, or exaltation, appearing in Isaiah 33:3 in the phrase 'at Your arising.' The context describes nations fleeing when God rises up in power. The term emphasizes the action of standing up or being lifted up, here applied to God's intervention in judgment. The root connects to elevation and exaltation, suggesting both physical rising and being honored or lifted in status. The nations scatter not just at God's presence but at His active arising to act.

senses.1: Uplifting, arising, or the act of rising up (Isaiah 33:3). The phrase 'at Your arising' describes God's action of standing up to intervene—nations flee when God rises from His throne to act in judgment. This is not static presence but active arising, suggesting movement from rest to action. The term combines physical rising with the exaltation that God's intervention brings. When God stands up, enemies scatter.
